title: Five friends, one circle
hook: Mutual friends could introduce you. Does it matter if they all know each other?

doesNotKnow: that the at-least-once rule needs independence
that friends from one circle rise and fall together

misconception: If each of 5 mutual friends has the same 10% chance of introducing you, the total chance is the same whether they all know each other or not.
objective: The learner can explain that five independent 10% chances give 41%, but five friends in one circle that meets half the weeks give only 34%, because their chances rise and fall together; each friend's own chance is still 10%.

claims.text: Five independent 10% chances give 1 - 0.9^5 = 41% of at least one success; you miss only if all five fail, and 0.9^5 = 59%.
claims.source: Arithmetic: 0.9^5 = 0.59049; model.ts separate() = 0.40951. Stage tick '41%: 5 separate circles'. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. 0.9^5 = 0.59049; 1 - 0.9^5 = 0.40951 -> 41% and 59%. Tick '41%: 5 separate circles' after the first chip.

claims.text: Stage model (stated on the card): the five friends' one circle meets in a share q of weeks; only in a meeting week can a friend introduce you, each independently with chance 10%/q, so each friend alone is still 10% a week. The chance you are introduced in a week is q(1 - (1 - 0.1/q)^5): 41% at q = 100%, 34% at 50%, 23% at 25%, 10% at 10%.
claims.source: model.ts oneCircle(); node 2026-10-14: 0.40951, 0.33616, 0.23056, 0.1. Seeded cross-check mulberry32(7), 10,000 weeks at q = 50%: 34.0%. Stage labels: 'Weeks the circle meets: n of 20 · then 20% each' (inMeetingWeek = 0.1/q). | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own: q(1 - (1 - 0.1/q)^5) = 0.40951, 0.33616, 0.23056, 0.1 at q = 1, .5, .25, .1 -> 41, 34, 23, 10%; meeting weeks 20, 10, 5, 2 of 20; 'then 20% each' at q = .5.

claims.text: When the circle meets in 10% of weeks, every friend introduces you in a meeting week (10%/10% = 100%), so the five act as one try: 10%.
Friends who share a circle are not independent tries: in the weeks the circle does not meet, all five fail at once, so counting them as separate tries overstates the chance.
claims.source: Under the stage model, P(all five fail) = (1 - q) + q(1 - 0.1/q)^5 > 0.9^5 for q < 1 (node: 0.664 at q = 0.5 vs 0.590), while each friend's marginal stays 0.1. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own: P(all fail) = (1 - q) + q(1 - 0.1/q)^5 = 0.664 at q = .5 vs 0.590 independent; the marginal stays 0.1. Verified in the stage model; the general sentence is the model's moral.

claims.text: The meeting-share model is a teaching model, not data about real friendships.
claims.source: Lesson rule (brief Round 3 item 2, planned claim 4). recall.question: Four friends each have a 20% chance of recommending you for a job. They all work in the same team, which is hiring only some years. Compared with four friends at four unrelated firms, your chance is:
recall.why: Friends in one team rise and fall together: in the years the team is not hiring, all four fail at once, so the at-least-once rule overstates the chance.
